## Q1 | The Butterbeer Tax

The Ministry of Magic was in some financial trouble after their considerable expenditures during the war. They decided to impose a tax of 6 galleons on the sale of butterbeer as a source of funding. The supply and demand curves for butterbeer can be represented by the following equations.

$$
D: P_B = 100 - \frac{1}{2} Q_D \qquad\qquad S: P_S = 20 + \frac{1}{2} Q_S
$$

Use a graph and algebra to illustrate what happened to the market before and after the tax. Start with the pre-tax equilibrium. Then use the tax equation ($P_B = \tau + P_S$) to solve for equilibrium quantity and the two prices. Conclude with the remaining relevant components.

::::: solution

Pre-Tax Price: $60$ galleons. Pre-Tax Quantity: $80$ bottles. Post-Tax Quantity: $74$ bottles. Buyer Price: $63$ galleons. Seller Price: $57$ galleons. Government Revenue: $444$ galleons. Deadweight Loss: $18$ galleons. Tax Incidence on Buyers: $3$. Tax Incidence on Sellers: $3$.

:::: {.columns gutter=1em}

::: column

Without the tax, buyers and sellers face one price:

$$
100 - \tfrac{1}{2} Q = 20 + \tfrac{1}{2} Q \quad\Rightarrow\quad Q = 80, \quad P = 60
$$

Before the tax, consumer surplus is the triangle above $60$, $\frac{1}{2} \times 80 \times 40 = 1600$, and producer surplus the triangle below it, also $\frac{1}{2} \times 80 \times 40 = 1600$.

With the tax, the buyer price sits $6$ above the seller price, and the market still clears at one quantity. Slide the $6$-galleon wedge in from the left until it gets stuck between the curves:

$$
P_B = 6 + P_S \quad\Rightarrow\quad 100 - \tfrac{1}{2} Q = 6 + (20 + \tfrac{1}{2} Q) \quad\Rightarrow\quad Q = 74
$$

so $P_B = 100 - 37 = 63$ and $P_S = 20 + 37 = 57$.

:::

::: column

![Tax equilibrium](data:image/svg+xml;base64,){width=100%}

:::

::::

Incidence: buyers pay $63 - 60 = 3$ more than before and sellers receive $60 - 57 = 3$ less. The two sides bear the tax equally because the curves are equally steep: neither side is better able to walk away than the other.

Welfare: consumer surplus shrinks from the triangle above $60$ to the triangle above $63$, $\frac{1}{2} \times 74 \times 37 = 1369$; producer surplus from the triangle below $60$ to the one below $57$, also $1369$. The rectangle between the two prices over the $74$ bottles still sold is government revenue, $6 \times 74 = 444$. The triangle between the curves over the $6$ bottles no longer sold is deadweight loss:

$$
\text{DWL} = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 6 \times (80 - 74) = 18
$$

Check: $1600 + 1600 = 1369 + 1369 + 444 + 18$.

:::::

## Q2 | The Butterbeer Subsidy

Now suppose that instead of the tax, the Ministry of Magic pays a 6 galleon subsidy on every butterbeer sold. Use a graph and algebra to discuss the impact of the subsidy on the market. Use the subsidy equation ($P_S = s + P_B$) to solve for equilibrium quantity, the two prices, and DWL.

::::

For the bottles sold beyond the pre-subsidy quantity, how does marginal benefit compare with marginal cost?

> a\) Marginal benefit is above marginal cost, so these added trades raise total surplus.
>
> b\) Marginal benefit is below marginal cost, so these added trades reduce total surplus once the Ministry’s spending is counted.
>
> c\) Marginal benefit equals marginal cost, so these added trades leave total surplus unchanged.
>
> d\) The subsidy lowers the sellers’ marginal cost, so these added trades cost society nothing.

::::: solution

Post-Subs Quantity: $86$ bottles. Deadweight Loss: $18$ galleons. Buyer Price: $57$ galleons. Seller Price: $63$ galleons. The choice is **b)**.

:::: {.columns gutter=1em}

::: column

A subsidy is the tax wedge turned around: the seller now receives $6$ more than the buyer pays, so the wedge sits to the *right* of the no-policy equilibrium:

$$
P_S = 6 + P_B \quad\Rightarrow\quad 20 + \tfrac{1}{2} Q = 6 + (100 - \tfrac{1}{2} Q) \quad\Rightarrow\quad Q = 86
$$

so $P_B = 100 - 43 = 57$ and $P_S = 20 + 43 = 63$.

:::

::: column

![Subsidy equilibrium](data:image/svg+xml;base64,){width=100%}

:::

::::

Both sides are better off: buyers pay $3$ less and sellers receive $3$ more, so consumer surplus rises from $1600$ to $\frac{1}{2} \times 86 \times 43 = 1849$ and producer surplus from $1600$ to $1849$. But the Ministry pays $6 \times 86 = 516$, more than the $249 + 249 = 498$ the buyers and sellers gain. The difference is the deadweight loss, the triangle between the curves over the six added bottles:

$$
\text{DWL} = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 6 \times (86 - 80) = 18
$$

**b)** Beyond the pre-subsidy $80$ bottles, supply (marginal cost) is above demand (marginal benefit). The $81$st through $86$th bottles cost $60.5$ to $63$ galleons to make, but buyers value them at only $59.5$ down to $57$; they are made only because the Ministry pays the gap. Counting the Ministry’s spending, each one lowers total surplus, by the $18$ above. Not a): that is the bottles *before* $80$. Not c): marginal benefit equals marginal cost only at $80$. Not d): the subsidy changes who pays the cost, not the cost itself; the Ministry’s galleons are a real cost to society.

:::::
